## Two worlds, one office

I work between finance and tech, and I have never seen this level of change in such a short period of time. What used to take me months and a team, I am now building alone in a few weeks.

And most people around me havenât seen what is happening yet, because for them, AI is simply a clever chatbot.

Strange as it may sound, I am spending my days in two worlds at once. In one, AI is doing the equivalent of a teamâs work. In the other, where most of the people I speak to every day live, itâs a search engine on steroids.

## AI is becoming more and more autonomous

The way I like to explain AI is by presenting it as a new colleague who gets better at the job month after month. In 2023, it could do simple tasks that took me a few minutes, like drafting an email. Now it can replace me in the vast majority of the tasks my team or I have to carry out.

This progress is actually being measured by a research group called METR . They give the AI real tasks, mostly in computer science and research, tasks an expert would spend hours on. They then let the AI work entirely on its own, and at the end someone checks whether the job got done. In November, their tests were no longer enough: the best models were passing them too easily. On a new, harder set, the models succeed about half the time at work that would take an expert some 27 hours. And the length of work they can handle doubles roughly every three and a half months. 2

On top of that, AI is already doing things no human has managed. In September, an OpenAI model put forward a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, an extremely complex problem about how fluids flow. It is one of the seven â Millennium Prize Problems ,â each worth a million dollars, and the institute that offers the prize says it has âapparentlyâ been solved. And yet, so far, mathematicians have learned almost nothing from it, because the proof is too hard for a human to understand. 3

We are in a period of history where AI produces knowledge faster than experts can understand it.

Anyone who still thinks AI is overhyped has most likely never tried to build something with it. The first time you do, you are blown away.

## Not in the numbers yet

Now if we look at the job numbers, even after nearly four years of ChatGPT being available to all, the very serious Yale Budget Lab still canât find AI in the US employment data. 4

In reality, the vast majority of people havenât really started using it yet. Andrej Karpathy , one of the people who helped build this technology, gave the best explanation Iâve read. 5 About six billion people have barely touched AI. Another one or two billion use a free chatbot now and then. Only around twenty million professionals use it for complex work. Those people, he says, feel âthe vertigo of the curve going vertical.â

But this is not new; we have been here before. Most technology revolutions follow a similar path. Take electricity: it took decades to show up in the productivity figures, because factories first had to be reorganized around it. The technology arrives in a few years, but the way we work, and the way we think, take much longer to change.

## A tide, not a tsunami

> Everyone is waiting for a tsunami. Whatâs coming is a tide, rising slowly.

There wonât be one big day to point at. Look at how itâs already moving.

First, the door closes before anyone walks in. Researchers at Stanford found that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the jobs most exposed to AI is 19% lower than it should be, mostly because fewer of them are being hired. 6

> For many, the problem wonât be losing a job. It will be finding one.

Then come the restructurings. In October, Microsoft offered buyouts to around 60,000 of its employees. In April, for the first time in its history, it had offered early retirement. 7 Neither announcement mentions AI. But I expect packages like these to be one of the ways companies cut jobs and replace them with AI. They cost less than layoffs and donât make the front page. Someone leaves, and the seat stays empty.

Each of these plans is a wave, and a big one for the people it carries off. Still, these waves hit one company at a time, months apart. Wave after wave, the tide rises.

Big tech, top consulting firms and banks will feel this first and hardest. Their work is digital, easy to check and very well paid, which is exactly where AI is strongest. Small firms and family businesses, which make up most of the economy, will change at their own pace.

## The question nobody answers

If companies stop hiring junior staff, how will they get the seniors they need in ten years?

I donât have a full answer, but what I currently think will happen is that the jobs we know will need to change, or new ones will appear. One of those I call the AI manager: the person who runs the machines, knows where they fail, and represents the team to the client. This role takes judgment and people skills more than any hard technical skill, because I think AI will be better than any human at the technical part.

If I were 23 today, thatâs what I would train for. And for anyone who manages a team, my advice is to always think hard about whether you need a junior or an AI for a specific role. These decisions canât be made lightly: a team that picks the AI every time will save money this year, but will have no one left to promote in five.

## The same song, faster

None of this is new. The steam engine, electricity, the internet: each one reached the lab long before it reached our lives, and hit some people years before others.

> Itâs the same song. Only faster.

The technology changes at the speed of computing power. People and companies change at the speed of people. That gap is where the trouble will be, and most of the opportunity too.

So if youâre uneasy, youâre right to be: youâve simply seen the tide before most people.
